title: The board underneath
intro: The motherboard is mostly wiring, and the interesting history is in what those wires connect to. Slots appear when a job is too big for the main processor and disappear when it absorbs the job back. Reading a board tells you what the machine could not do on its own.

blocks.title: One shared bus, and everybody waits their turn
blocks.text: A bus is a set of wires that every expansion card listens to. In the original design all cards shared one path running at the speed of the slowest thing on it, which was fine when a card was a serial port and impossible once cards were pushing video.

blocks.name: ISA, 8-bit
blocks.text: IBM published the specification, so anyone could build a card. That decision created the entire PC industry, and it also meant IBM could not stop others from building the whole machine.

blocks.name: ISA, 16-bit
blocks.text: A second connector added behind the first, so old 8-bit cards still fitted. Backward compatibility by physically extending the slot, which is a very PC solution.

blocks.name: IBM Micro Channel
blocks.text: IBM's attempt to reclaim the standard with a faster bus that required paying royalties. Manufacturers refused, formed a rival group, and IBM's own architecture became a minority option on its own platform.

blocks.name: EISA
blocks.text: The industry's answer to Micro Channel: as fast, no licence, and it accepted existing cards. Expensive enough that it stayed mostly in servers.

blocks.name: VESA Local Bus
blocks.text: A slot wired almost directly to the 486's own bus, which made it fast and extremely fussy. It was tied to one processor generation and died with it in about two years.

blocks.name: PCI
blocks.text: Fast, not tied to any one processor, and it configured cards automatically instead of requiring you to set switches on the card by hand. Plug and Play started here, and PCI outlasted every bus that came before it.

blocks.title: The shape of the modern machine
blocks.text: ATX set the physical layout still in use today, and a dedicated graphics slot appeared because one card had outgrown everything else. This is also the period when the board split into two support chips, a fast one near the processor and a slow one for everything else.

blocks.name: ATX form factor
blocks.spec: 305 x 244 mm, rear I/O panel, software power off
blocks.text: Thirty years on, this machine uses the same standard. It moved the connectors to a single rear panel, put the processor where the power supply fan could reach it, and let the operating system switch the machine off, which the older AT design could not do.

blocks.name: USB 1.0
blocks.text: Before this, a mouse, a keyboard, a printer and a modem each used a different connector, and adding one often meant opening the case and setting a card's interrupt number by hand. Slow to be adopted, and then it replaced everything.

blocks.name: AGP
blocks.spec: 1x at 266 MB/s, rising to 8x at 2.1 GB/s by 2002
blocks.text: A slot for one card only, wired straight to the memory controller, because graphics had become the one device that could saturate PCI on its own.

blocks.name: Northbridge and southbridge
blocks.spec: Two chips: fast memory and graphics, slow everything else
blocks.text: The board's support logic split in two. The northbridge sat near the processor handling memory and the graphics slot, the southbridge handled drives, USB and audio. Both have since been absorbed, the northbridge into the processor and the southbridge into a single chipset.

blocks.name: USB 2.0
blocks.text: Forty times faster, which is what made external hard drives and memory sticks practical and killed the floppy disk.

blocks.title: Point to point, and the slow disappearance of the slot
blocks.text: PCI Express is not a shared bus. Every device gets its own dedicated pair of wires in each direction, called a lane, and gets as many lanes as it needs. That change removed the last reason for separate buses, and everything on a modern board is now some number of PCIe lanes.

blocks.name: Serial ATA
blocks.text: The ribbon cable that had run from the board to the drives since 1986 finally went.

blocks.name: PCI Express 1.0
blocks.spec: 250 MB/s per lane, x1 to x16 slots
blocks.text: Cards get exactly the bandwidth they need and none of it is shared. A x16 graphics slot and a x1 sound card sit on the same standard, differing only in how many lanes are wired to them.

blocks.name: Memory controller moves onto the processor
blocks.text: The northbridge's main job went into the processor itself, cutting a whole chip out of the path between the processor and its memory. It also means the memory types a board supports are decided by the processor, not the board.

blocks.name: PCIe 2.0
blocks.spec: 500 MB/s per lane, 8 GB/s at x16
blocks.text: Each generation of PCI Express has roughly doubled the rate per lane while keeping the same physical slot, so a new card fits an old board and simply runs slower.

blocks.name: USB 3.0
blocks.text: Ten times USB 2.0, which made external SSDs sensible and started the long process of one connector doing everything.

blocks.name: PCIe 3.0
blocks.spec: ~1 GB/s per lane, 16 GB/s at x16
blocks.text: Current for eight years, and still enough for most graphics cards well after it was superseded.

blocks.name: UEFI replaces BIOS
blocks.spec: Graphical setup, GPT partitions, drives over 2 TB, secure boot
blocks.text: The BIOS dated to 1981 and could not boot from a drive larger than 2.2 TB. UEFI is closer to a small operating system that runs before the real one, which brought mouse support and pretty menus, and also brought signed boot images and the arguments about who controls them.

blocks.name: M.2
blocks.spec: PCIe x4 or SATA, 22 x 80 mm, no cable
blocks.text: A slot flat on the board for a drive with no cable and no power lead. It is where the storage in this machine lives, under the graphics card.

blocks.name: The last ISA-descended slot goes
blocks.text: Conventional PCI slots quietly stopped appearing on consumer boards, twenty-four years after the standard arrived and thirty-six after the original ISA slot it descended from.

blocks.name: PCIe 4.0
blocks.text: Fast enough that board makers had to start using better circuit board materials and adding signal repeaters, because the copper traces themselves were losing the signal over the distance.

blocks.name: PCIe 5.0
blocks.spec: ~4 GB/s per lane, 64 GB/s at x16
blocks.text: The current standard, and the reason this board can run a graphics card and two storage drives without any of them slowing the others down.

blocks.name: What is left on the board
blocks.spec: One socket, four memory slots, two PCIe slots, two M.2 slots
blocks.text: Compare that to a 1996 board with six or seven slots, all of them likely to be occupied. Sound, networking, USB, storage control and graphics output are all built in now. The empty slot on this machine is the honest summary of forty years of progress.
